title: Social-protection formalization requires affordability and human navigation, not information alone
source_unit: International Labour Organization, What Drives Social Security Registration? Experimental Evidence from Behavioural Interventions in Jordan’s Estidama++ Programme, 2026
geography: Jordan; small firms with 1–9 registered workers and eligible Jordanian and non-Jordanian workers in the Estidama++ programme

observations.period: 2024–2025; randomised evaluation of firm outreach and SMS interventions

denominator.unit: Jordanian social-security registration system and Estidama++ programme

coverage_gap.unit: percent of workers in Jordan remaining unprotected by social security

firm_visit_effect.unit: additional workers per firm registered in SSC 1.5 years after in-person visits

relative_effect.unit: percent more registered workers per firm than firms not visited

mechanism.value: human outreach increased registration mainly by making the subsidized programme and its affordability legible, rather than by increasing employment

observations.method: Randomized controlled trial: 800 firms received in-person visits and 1,646 firms served as comparison; outcomes were followed for 1.5 years. The brief also reports a separate SMS experiment covering 29,372 treatment firms and 14,685 comparison firms.
observations.uncertainty: The experiment concerns eligible small firms and a temporary subsidy in Jordan; registration is an administrative coverage outcome, not proof of benefit adequacy, long-run retention, improved job quality, or household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Informal and low-income workers, women, non-Jordanian workers and refugees, small firms, employers, and workers with limited contributory capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: The treatment may have changed take-up of a subsidized programme more than underlying willingness to contribute to ordinary social insurance; results may differ when subsidies expire or for firms outside the eligible small-firm frame.

observations.period: February 2024–April 2024; information design and institutional engagement

denominator.unit: firms randomly selected for in-person visits

programme_awareness.value: among visited firms, awareness that Estidama++ was a subsidy rose to 49% versus 29% among non-visited comparison firms; knowledge of all eligibility criteria was 17% versus 10%

portal_engagement.unit: percent higher monthly SSC logins for visited firms in April 2025

process_friction.value: visits did not improve perceived ease of registration or contribution, and firms still reported difficulty managing, updating and uploading worker information

mechanism.value: personalized explanation can create institutional engagement while leaving the administrative interface itself hard to use

observations.method: Behaviourally informed face-to-face outreach by 50 trained Social Security Corporation officials, using a simplified brochure, step-by-step guidance, reminders, and monitored visits; comparison with eligible firms without visits.
observations.uncertainty: Knowledge and login measures are intermediate outcomes; the brief does not establish whether improved engagement translated into sustained contribution payment, claim use, or greater trust after the programme ended.
observations.subgroup: Small-firm owners, administrative staff, workers navigating registration, and institutions serving people with low digital or bureaucratic capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Human contact may partly reflect the authority or credibility of an official visit rather than the content of the behavioural message; simplifying information without simplifying the process may have limited value.

observations.period: 2024–2025; comparison of scalable digital outreach with intensive human outreach

denominator.unit: firms randomly selected for SMS treatment

sms_registration.value: SMS produced a small positive effect on Estidama++ uptake but no effect on the number of workers registered into SSC

sms_cost.unit: JOD per firm for nine SMS messages

visit_cost.unit: JOD per additional firm participating in Estidama++ through firm visits

channel_tradeoff.value: SMS is substantially cheaper and scalable but weak for worker registration; firm visits are costly but effective, implying a complementary outreach mix

mechanism.value: digital reach can distribute information cheaply, while human assistance is needed when affordability, eligibility, trust, and administrative friction must be resolved together

observations.method: Randomized comparison of positively framed and loss-aversion SMS campaigns with a no-SMS comparison group, alongside the randomized in-person visit intervention; reported cost-effectiveness calculations.
observations.uncertainty: Costs exclude staff wages and results depend on Jordan’s existing outreach infrastructure; the study does not identify the optimal mix for other programmes, populations, languages, or benefit systems.
observations.subgroup: Workers and firms with weak digital access, limited time, low trust, low financial room, or complex administrative needs; public agencies balancing reach and casework capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: SMS may work better when paired with a simpler registration interface or larger benefits; the null worker-registration effect could reflect temporary subsidy design or employer-level rather than worker-level bottlenecks.

boundary: This record adds randomized evidence that in-person outreach plus temporary contribution subsidies increased social-security registration among eligible Jordanian small firms, while SMS alone did not increase worker registration. It does not establish benefit adequacy, durable post-subsidy coverage, job quality, household welfare, or generalizability beyond the Jordanian small-firm and Estidama++ context.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO brief and publication/project pages, 52% unprotected-worker context, Estidama++ subsidy design, randomized firm-visit and SMS samples, registration effects, knowledge and login outcomes, process friction, cost comparison, and post-subsidy boundary were reviewed.
